presentingComplaint: 48 hours of high fever, worsening confusion and a witnessed seizure, now hypotensive and requiring vasopressor support.
history: Previously well 58-year-old man, non-diabetic, brought to the emergency department after 2 days of high-grade fever and progressive behavioural change noted by his family - initially irritability and word-finding difficulty, then disorientation to time and place. This morning he had a witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting ~2 minutes followed by post-ictal drowsiness. Over the preceding few hours he became increasingly obtunded, mottled and clammy, prompting emergency transfer. No prior neurological disease, no recent travel, no immunosuppression, no injection drug use. No neck trauma. No obvious source of systemic sepsis on collateral history (no urinary, respiratory or abdominal symptoms). No sick contacts, no animal or tick exposure. Not on anticoagulants or steroids.
examination: Toxic, poorly responsive man. GCS E2V3M5 (10/15), disoriented, intermittently agitated. Temperature 39.4°C, peripherally shut down with prolonged capillary refill and mottled knees. Mild nuchal discomfort but no frank meningism; Kernig negative. Expressive dysphasia and a subtle right facial droop with right pronator drift consistent with left temporal lobe involvement. No papilloedema. No rash, no petechiae. Chest clear, abdomen soft and non-tender, no focus of infection identified. Post-ictal but no ongoing seizure activity.
imaging: MRI brain: T2/FLAIR hyperintensity with gyral swelling and restricted diffusion involving the left medial temporal lobe, insula and inferior frontal cortex, with early petechial haemorrhage - a pattern highly characteristic of herpes simplex encephalitis. No abscess, no mass with rim enhancement, no hydrocephalus.
microbiology: Two sets of peripheral blood cultures drawn before antimicrobials: no growth at 48h. CSF bacterial culture: no growth. CSF HSV-1 PCR: POSITIVE (high copy number). CSF enterovirus and VZV PCR negative. CSF cryptococcal antigen negative. Serum procalcitonin only mildly elevated, inconsistent with bacterial sepsis. EEG: periodic lateralised epileptiform discharges (PLEDs) over the left temporal region.
differentialDiagnoses: Herpes simplex (HSV-1) encephalitis with septic-shock physiology from the neuro-inflammatory insult and seizure
finalDiagnosis: Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) encephalitis with associated shock and multi-organ dysfunction (AKI, thrombocytopenia, hyperlactataemia).
citations: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Acute Viral Encephalitis
Surviving Sepsis Campaign - Adult Sepsis and Septic Shock - 2021
stewardship: This is a neurological emergency in a haemodynamically unstable host: start empiric IV aciclovir immediately (do NOT wait for CSF PCR) at 10 mg/kg every 8h (adjusted for AKI), because delay in aciclovir worsens outcome in HSV encephalitis. Because bacterial meningoencephalitis cannot be excluded at presentation and the patient is in shock, give concurrent empiric antibacterials per meningitis pathway - IV ceftriaxone 2g q12h PLUS vancomycin (loaded, level-guided) - after paired blood cultures and, once safe, lumbar puncture. Manage shock in parallel per Surviving Sepsis (balanced fluids, early noradrenaline to MAP ≥65, lactate clearance). CULTURE-DIRECTED DE-ESCALATION: with CSF HSV-1 PCR positive, negative CSF Gram stain/culture, negative blood cultures at 48h, normal CSF:serum glucose ratio and only mildly raised procalcitonin, STOP ceftriaxone and vancomycin and continue aciclovir monotherapy to complete a 14-21 day course, repeating CSF HSV PCR near end of therapy to confirm clearance before stopping.
contraindications: Avoid aciclovir underdosing but reduce dose/extend interval for AKI (CrCl-adjusted) to prevent crystal nephropathy and neurotoxicity
Ensure adequate hydration with aciclovir to limit renal tubular crystallisation, especially with existing AKI
Do not delay aciclovir for imaging or LP if there is any contraindication to immediate LP
Avoid nephrotoxic combinations where possible; monitor vancomycin levels closely given concurrent AKI
edgeCases: Early MRI and even initial CSF HSV PCR can be falsely negative in the first 72h - repeat PCR at 3-7 days if suspicion remains high and continue aciclovir meanwhile

Septic-shock physiology here is driven by the encephalitic/systemic inflammatory response and seizure rather than bacteraemia, so a negative septic screen should not prompt hunting for antibiotics but should trigger antibacterial de-escalation
Autoimmune (anti-NMDA-receptor) encephalitis can mimic or follow HSV encephalitis - consider if no improvement or relapse after appropriate antiviral therapy
expectedMaiK: Fever + rapidly progressive encephalopathy with focal temporal-lobe features (dysphasia, personality change, seizure) plus CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis with red cells and characteristic left medial temporal MRI signal indicate HSV encephalitis; empiric aciclovir must start at once, with empiric antibacterial meningitis cover and sepsis resuscitation given the shock, then antibacterials de-escalated once CSF HSV PCR is positive and bacterial cultures are negative.
expectedNextQuestions: Time of onset and progression of the confusion, and any preceding behavioural or psychiatric change?
Any focal neurological symptoms, speech disturbance or seizure activity?
Immunosuppression, HIV risk, recent travel, animal/tick/mosquito exposure or vaccination status?
Any features of raised intracranial pressure or contraindication to lumbar puncture?
expectedInvestigations: Urgent CT head then lumbar puncture with CSF cell count, protein, glucose, Gram stain and culture
MRI brain with diffusion and contrast
Paired blood cultures, lactate, renal and liver profile, coagulation and procalcitonin
regressionAssertions: Engine must rank ENCEPHALITIS as the top diagnosis given fever, focal temporal-lobe encephalopathy, seizure and characteristic CSF/MRI.
Empiric plan must include IV aciclovir started without waiting for PCR.
Empiric bacterial meningitis cover (ceftriaxone + vancomycin) must be present at presentation given shock and diagnostic uncertainty.
Once CSF HSV PCR is positive with negative bacterial cultures, antibacterials must be de-escalated/stopped and aciclovir continued for 14-21 days.
Shock must be managed per sepsis pathway without attributing it to occult bacteraemia after negative cultures.
